description: We conduct research and build games that make real space science playable. Our team leader, Grayson DeLuca, is a fourth Grade student at Clemmons Elementary School in North Carolina, USA. He is scheduled to attend NASA space camp this summer! His partner is his father, who is an engineer and researcher.
summary:
Survive In Space is a browser game where kids ages 7–12 run humanity’s first outpost at Shackleton crater on the Moon’s south pole. Every choice costs something. Player's race across the lunar surface collecting power cells, ice, food and rare minerals, with only eight backpack slots. Each night they decide which systems lose power: life support, greenhouse, lab, radio, launch pad or storage. Daily missions send them to rescue a lost rover, fix a power relay or recover a crashed probe. When a real solar flare from NASA’s records hits, they have seconds to reach a radiation shelter.

The game turns the challenge’s core trade-offs into play: life support, radiation shielding, power, food and communication delay. It’s built on NASA DONKI space-weather data (live and archived), OSDR and RadLab radiation measurements, Moon Trek terrain and the Canadian Space Agency’s food toolkit. Each day ends by explaining the real science, with links to the sources.

Kids don’t just learn that space is hard. They feel the trade-offs mission planners face, and start thinking like them. Play free at surviveinspace.earth.
details:
Survive In Space is a free browser game that puts kids ages 7 to 12 in charge of humanity's first outpost at Shackleton crater on the Moon's south pole for seven days, where every choice costs something. Players explore lunar terrain in a side-scrolling platformer. They jump craters, dodge aliens and collect power cells, ice, food, rock samples, orange glass beads, ilmenite and helium-3, but their backpack holds only eight items, so every trip forces a decision about what matters most. Back at base, they walk into the habitat, greenhouse, science lab, radio room, storage and launch pad to deliver supplies. Each night they choose which systems stay powered: the generator can run four of the six systems, but once its fuel runs out, solar panels can run only three. This mirrors the real problem of surviving the 14-day lunar night. Solar flares in the game are real NASA-recorded events, such as the X5.1 flare of November 11, 2025. When one strikes, players have seconds to reach a radiation shelter, and their dose is tracked against a safety limit. Daily missions send them to rescue a lost rover, fix a power relay or recover a crashed probe, and an unfinished mission carries over to the next day. Players can also ship Moon resources to Earth for coins and save up for a radar, drill, scout rover or Moon car. Every day ends by explaining the real science behind what just happened, and a Real NASA data page links to every source. A shared leaderboard with kid-safe generated nicknames keeps only each player's best score and lets players jump straight to their own rank.

The main benefit is that kids learn mission planning by doing it, weighing the same trade-offs NASA engineers face between life support, radiation shielding, power, food and communication. The game runs in any browser, with nothing to install and no account required. That makes it easy to use in classrooms, at home or in libraries, and an offline single-file version is available for schools with limited internet. Because every in-game fact is sourced, teachers can use it as a launch point for real STEM lessons. Our intended impact is for kids to leave thinking like mission planners, seeing space exploration as a set of connected decisions with real consequences. That systems thinking about limited resources also applies on Earth, to energy, food and disaster preparedness. Next we plan to add a Mars mode with a 4 to 24 minute communication delay, a teacher guide and classroom leaderboards.

We built the game in JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas and CSS, with Node.js serverless functions. It is hosted on Netlify, which uses Netlify Functions for the leaderboard API and the NASA data connection, and Netlify Blobs for score storage. The code is managed on GitHub and the game is served at surviveinspace.earth. The game draws on NASA DONKI space-weather data (a live feed plus archived flare events), NASA OSDR and RadLab radiation data, NASA Moon Trek terrain for Shackleton crater, the Canadian Space Agency's food-in-space toolkit, and published lunar radiation measurements from the Chang'e-4 lander. We created a code-rendered cinematic intro encoded with FFmpeg and used Playwright for automated testing on desktop and mobile, including bot players that ran 60 levels to confirm every level can be beaten. Development was AI-assisted using Anthropic's Claude, and any AI-generated audio or video is labeled as such.

What makes Moonbase Run creative is that the science is the gameplay rather than a quiz added on top. Kids experience radiation shielding when a real flare forces them into a shelter, and they feel the weight of power trade-offs when they must choose between the greenhouse and the lab for the night. Real data drives the story, since the flares players survive actually happened, with dates and links to prove it. Missions that carry over and savings goals teach kids to plan ahead instead of only reacting. In designing it, we focused on age fit, with simple controls, short levels, readable text and touch buttons for phones. We also focused on child privacy: there are no accounts, no typed names and no personal data, and the leaderboard relies on generated nicknames and anonymous device IDs stored only as one-way hashes. We held to scientific honesty by never presenting archived data as live and by clearly labeling pretend elements like aliens and coins. To keep the leaderboard fair, the server recalculates every score, rejects impossible results and limits how often scores can be posted. And to keep it accessible, the game is free, runs on low-end devices and has an offline version.
